80889.subject: On Quantum Risk
80889.body:
View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/eaa70932-7ce4-467e-b338-a662ed575d6a/0xR_NL_Banner_Heading_Wordmark.jpg?t=1776775276)
Caption: 

Last week, Luke [covered](https://blockworks-research.beehiiv.com/p/bunker-mode?_bhlid=e5a47cb5c433086b01b4c4bd8a3544ff8cfd77c3) the AI side of Justin Drake’s “[bunker mode](https://x.com/drakefjustin/status/2107837081313505768)” argument. One of the [replies](https://x.com/rcarback/status/2107973165343236360?s=20) to Drake’s post came from [Dr. Richard Carback](https://www.linkedin.com/in/richard-carback/) of Postquant Labs, who said that he thinks quantum will get there before AI does, but the timeline is under two years either way. I recently had the opportunity to sit in on a lecture of his, where the central premise of the discussion was his belief that cryptographically relevant quantum computers (CRQCs), quantum computers powerful enough to break the public-key cryptography used by most blockchains and much of the internet, will be a reality much sooner than most industry estimates predict. 

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/6ae63aad-536a-4e61-9908-019b52b1984c/image.png?t=1792063876)
Caption: 

Carback’s own [Quantum Doom Clock](https://quantumdoomclock.com/) currently places this inflection point on March 8th 2028, while another [calculator](https://ecdsa.fail/) from Eigen Labs places the current frontier ~67% ahead of Google's most recently disclosed quantum circuit. The most-cited industry benchmark is the [Global Risk Institute's annual Quantum Threat Timeline](https://globalriskinstitute.org/publication/quantum-threat-timeline-report-2025b/), which placed the odds of a viable CRQC at 28-49% by 2035 and 51-70% by 2040, though this survey assessed the likelihood of RSA-2048 being broken, not secp256k1, which is where the technology is more relevant to crypto. 

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/d5206cc4-b448-477d-909b-c057870c31d6/image.png?t=1792063874)
Caption: 

The true timeline relies on the answer to how many qubits can be fit into a circuit, and how many qubits are needed to break a given encryption standard. Earlier this year, Google Quantum AI published a [paper](https://quantumai.google/static/site-assets/downloads/cryptocurrency-whitepaper.pdf) with the EF’s Justin Drake attesting that an attacker would need fewer than 500K physical qubits, invalidating the widely held industry estimate of 10-20M, while a companion report from Oratomic (Caltech and Harvard) suggested that a neutral-atom machine could achieve the same result with ~10K qubits. Thus, the timeline has accelerated dramatically in 2026 as the maximum number of physical qubits on a circuit has increased while the number of qubits needed to carry out

80805.subject: More Trading, Different Activity: Avalanche’s Latest 30 Days
80805.body:
View this post on the web at https://www.team1.blog/p/more-trading-different-activity-avalanches

Nansen recorded 48.4 million transactions, down 33% from the previous 30 days. At the same time, DEX volume climbed to $2.7 billion, up 145%, while active users increased 8.1% to 1.6 million.
So Avalanche was not simply quieter. There were fewer transactions in Nansen’s dataset, but much more trading volume. Users still grew, capital continued moving through the ecosystem, and activity across individual Avalanche L1s adds another part of the picture.
Trading picked up fast
The biggest change is DEX volume. WAVAX alone accounted for around $2.5 billion, with roughly $1.3 billion in buys and $1.3 billion in sells.
Active users also moved higher, reaching around 1.6 million, up 8.1% from the previous period. If that user growth continues while transactions stabilize, this month may end up looking more like a change in how Avalanche is being used than a simple drop in activity.
Want to keep up with the latest in the Avalanche ecosystem? Subscribe to the Team1 blog and get our updates in your inbox weekly.
AVAX and WAVAX are moving differently
Around $4.6 million of native AVAX left exchange wallets over the latest seven days. WAVAX went the other way. Around $12.3 million moved into exchanges, while Top PnL wallets reduced their WAVAX positions by roughly $2.2 million.
Native AVAX is moving away from exchanges while WAVAX is moving toward them. At the same time, WAVAX remains extremely active on DEXs. For now, it looks more like capital moving around the ecosystem than everyone taking the same position.
Fresh wallets are still bringing money in
Fresh wallets added approximately $20.8 million in AVAX over seven days. Another $16.3 million went into WAVAX. Those are meaningful inflows, but both were below their normal levels. AVAX was running at around 0.6x its average flow, while WAVAX was around 0.4x.
New wallets are participating, just not at an unusually high rate. There is fresh capital coming in, but this does not look like another sudden wave of adoption.
BTC.b is still doing real volume
BTC.b continues to be one of the more active parts of Avalanche DeFi. It recorded around $238.8 million in DEX volume over 30 days, with approximately $1.3 million in net flow.
Over the latest seven days, BTC.b generated another $60.9 million in volume, with $31.5 million in buys and $29.4 million in sells.
There is no major imbalance between buyers and sellers. It is simply an active market.
Bitcoin liquidity gives Avalanche another source of capital beyond AVAX and stablecoins, and BTC.b is still moving through the ecosystem rather than simply sitting in wallets.
sAVAX looks steady
sAVAX has around 16,609 holders, approximately $169.8 million in market cap, and roughly $2.2 million in liquidity. Seven-day volume was around $743,000, with approximately $424,000 in buys compared with $319,000 in sells.
There is no obvious new staking surge here.
